part_title: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, Structured Prompts and RAG
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 08–11 individually; confirmed ticket labels, few-shot examples, AWS storage comparison, retrieval excerpts and citations.

scenes.title: Zero-shot prompting
scenes.narration: Zero-shot prompting means asking a model to perform a task without showing it labeled examples in that prompt. Follow the slide from left to right. First, the instruction defines three possible categories: Billing, Account access and Technical. In the middle, a new support ticket says 'I cannot sign in.' The model uses its existing language understanding to interpret the request, then the final panel shows its predicted label, Account access. No training job runs and the model's weights do not change. This can be a quick way to start tasks such as classification, summarization and extraction when the model already understands the instruction. But the result still needs evaluation. For example, a request about a failed payment should normally map to Billing, while an app that crashes may fit Technical. If you find that the labels are inconsistent, improve the category descriptions or move to few-shot prompting, which the next slide demonstrates. The important takeaway is that zero-shot does not mean zero context: you still need a clear task, defined labels and a realistic input. It means you have not supplied completed examples of the task.

scenes.title: Few-shot prompting
scenes.narration: Few-shot prompting adds a handful of worked examples directly to a prompt. Look at the left panel: the model receives a classification instruction with the same Billing, Account access and Technical labels as before. Three sample tickets teach the pattern. 'My invoice is wrong' maps to Billing. 'I cannot sign in to my account' maps to Account access. 'The app keeps crashing' maps to Technical. Then the new input says 'I was charged twice.' The middle panel shows the model using those examples as context to infer the correct category, Billing. The right-hand table keeps category names consistent across the examples and the new answer. That consistency matters; if you alternate between 'Payments' and 'Billing' for identical cases, the model may learn an ambiguous pattern. Look at the comparison below: few-shot prompting is in-context learning, so it does not update model weights. Fine-tuning instead uses a separate training process to update weights for supported models. Begin with clear examples when you need more consistent behavior than zero-shot prompting provides, then measure whether the improvement justifies the extra prompt tokens and cost.

scenes.title: Structured reasoning prompts: concept and limits
scenes.narration: This slide teaches a way to organize complex tasks into checkable steps. The clipboard on the left lists four checkpoints: identify requirements, compare suitable options, check constraints, and give a concise justified recommendation. The example question asks which AWS storage type suits application logs. In the next panel, the prompt asks the model to examine data size, access patterns, retention, durability and cost before recommending a service. Follow the third panel. For large log volumes written once and read infrequently, Amazon S3 may be appropriate because it provides durable, scalable object storage. The alternatives shown are EFS for shared file systems, EBS for block storage attached to compute, and FSx for managed file-system workloads. The decision also checks archival policies and governance constraints. The far-right panel explains the limit: a structured response can still make wrong assumptions or omit requirements. You should request a short justification, key assumptions, sources and calculations that can be independently checked. The slide specifically advises against relying on hidden internal reasoning. A readable decision summary with verifiable evidence is more useful for architecture review than a long, unverified explanation.

scenes.title: Ground prompts with retrieval
scenes.narration: This diagram shows how to ground a model's answer in approved company documents. Start with the user question: 'How do I request access to an internal tool?' Instead of guessing, the system retrieves an Access Request Guide, an Account Setup FAQ and other relevant policies. In the third panel, the prompt includes excerpts from these documents as clearly separated context and instructs the model to use those sources. The example guide says to submit an access request through the internal portal with manager approval. The FAQ says account provisioning typically takes two to three business days. Follow the arrow to the final answer, which combines those facts and cites source one and source two. This is retrieval-augmented generation: external information is provided during the request without changing model weights. Notice the document dates from 2024. They are examples, but they also show why freshness matters. If the access process changed, a citation to an old guide could still mislead the employee. Review relevance, completeness, permissions and document dates, and refresh the source material when needed. Grounding improves traceability; it does not automatically guarantee correctness.
